rationale: The report's centre of gravity — direct reading of the Medina 1894 edition of Carvajal and of Oviedo's redaction — cannot enter this pass: the only retrieved texts for those works are archive.org item pages (bibliographic metadata, copyright status, download options), not the OCR. Every quotation the report attributes to Medina pp. 8–54 or Oviedo pp. 552–558 is therefore unshown here and is dispositioned blocked with the download route, not written into the ledger. What the item pages do allow: a url correction on SRC-CARVAJAL-1542 (the ledger holds it key-less; the page confirms the work, editor, publisher, and year) and a provisional, unverified Source record for Oviedo t. IV so the witness has a home when its text is read. The report's declared failure — Peripato et al. 2023 could not be opened — is reversed by the packet: the accepted manuscript was retrieved via an open-access repository and is read here in full. It supplies six new observation claims (LiDAR discovery count, basin-wide undiscovered-earthwork prediction, the low-probability share of the basin, the Acre concentration, the domesticated-species association, and the deforestation/road sampling bias), a comparator to AMZ-C004's regional prediction, independent corroboration of AMZ-C020/C016 on proportion, and a second, independent statement that Acre earthworks date to AD 120–400 (qualifying AMZ-C017). Independence is flagged: Peripato shares authors with three ledger sources. No edition change: the text-critical rewrite the report wants depends on quotations not yet in hand, and Peripato deepens the record without altering the telling.

sources.title: More than 10,000 pre-Columbian earthworks are still hidden throughout Amazonia
reliabilityNotes: Text read from the accepted manuscript (author version) deposited at White Rose Research Online (https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/207653/1/Vinicius_et_al_2023_Science_AAM.pdf), reached via OpenAlex; page locators cite that PDF, not the journal pagination. The manuscript title reads 'Over 10,000…'; the deposit record gives the published title used here.
Internal inconsistency to note: the abstract gives the predicted range as 10,272–23,640 undiscovered sites; the main text (p. 7) gives 10,272–23,648.

Not independent of several ledger sources: shares authors with SRC-LEVIS-2017 (Levis), SRC-DESOUZA-2018 (de Souza, Iriarte), SRC-LOMBARDO-2025 (Lombardo, Iriarte), and draws its 'domesticated species' list from Levis et al. 2017. Treat as the same research network as those records for independence grouping.

Presence-only archaeological data with acknowledged sampling bias toward deforested, road-accessible areas; the model corrects for this with observability covariates, but the correction is itself modelled.
Authors declare no competing interests; funding from Brazilian public agencies (CAPES, FAPESP, CNPq) and ERC (PAST project).

Oviedo's version of the Orellana descent is a sixteenth-century compiler's redaction of Carvajal's account, not an independent eyewitness: it is a distinct manuscript witness to the same source (relevant to AMZ-C002), and Oviedo also vouches personally for Carvajal (credibility evidence, not diagnosticity — per the report, unverified).
Nineteenth-century edition of a sixteenth-century manuscript; editorial normalisation of spelling possible ('mill', 'ginco' in OCR per the report).

evidence.title: Basin-wide LiDAR (5,315 km², 0.08% of Amazonia) revealed 24 previously unreported earthworks
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states that inspection of 5,315 km² of airborne LiDAR transects, originally flown for biomass estimation, "revealed 24 unreported earthworks in southern, southwestern, central, and northern" Amazonia, including a plaza town in the Upper Xingu, geoglyphs in Acre, features in Amapá, and two floodplain earthworks in central Amazonia. The supplement adds that nine already-catalogued earthworks were also seen, that the 33 records fell on 12 of 861 flight lines, and that the resulting density was 0.0062 earthworks/km².
evidence.editorInference: A direct count from a dataset not designed for archaeology, which is what makes it usable as a quasi-unbiased sample; but 0.08% coverage and clustering on 12 of 861 lines mean the raw density is unstable, as the authors themselves say when they reject naive extrapolation.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 5] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints); supplement [p. 39]
limitations: Coverage is 0.08% of the basin; the 200 m transect width truncates features.
Roughly half of the features flagged by the viewer were confirmed by archaeological experts (supplement p. 35); confirmation was by expert judgement, not excavation.

evidence.title: Inhomogeneous Poisson model predicts 10,272–23,648 undiscovered earthworks basin-wide
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states that its model "predicts the number of yet undiscovered pre-Columbian structures as 10,272" to 23,648 with 95% probability (mean 16,187), so that documented earthworks account for 4–9% of the total "and that 91 – 96% of Amazonian earthworks remain undiscovered." The model used 937 known earthworks plus the 24 new ones, nine environmental covariates, and observability covariates (road distance, tree cover) to weight sampling bias. The paper first notes that naive extrapolation of the observed density would give over 41,000 earthworks, and rejects that figure as not accounting for uneven distribution.
evidence.editorInference: The paper's own move from 41,000 (naive) to 10–24k (modelled) illustrates how strongly earthwork totals depend on the estimator — the same lesson AMZ-C005 and AMZ-C012 draw for population. The abstract's upper bound (23,640) and the main text's (23,648) differ by a typographical margin.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 6]–[p. 7] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints)
limitations: Prediction from presence-only data; the bias correction is modelled, not measured.
'Earthworks' here means ring ditches, geoglyphs, ponds, and wells — not mounds, dark earths, or raised fields — so the count is not commensurable with all 'site' totals in the record.

evidence.title: Comparator: a basin-wide 10–24k undiscovered-earthwork prediction beside the Aquiry 24–30k regional prediction
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states that its model "predicts the number of yet undiscovered pre-Columbian structures as 10,272" to 23,648 for the whole 6.7 million km² basin, and that nearly all highest-probability cells fall in a 94,713 km² "rectangle that overlays a significant portion of the Brazilian state of Acre."
evidence.editorInference: Editor's comparison: SRC-PARSSINEN-2026 predicts roughly 24,000–30,000 earthworks within a ~183,000 km² Aquiry area alone — more than Peripato's upper bound for the entire basin, over an area about twice Peripato's high-probability rectangle. The two are not strictly commensurable (different earthwork definitions, data, and estimators; Peripato's 2023 model predates the 2026 LiDAR), so this does not undermine what AMZ-C004 states the 2026 study predicts. It does show that earthwork totals differ several-fold between published models, which AMZ-R004-style dependency work should address. Zero diagnosticity for the truth of C004 as worded; logged as the comparator the report sought.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 7] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints)
limitations: Different operational definitions of 'earthwork' and different survey data between the two studies.
Peripato's model predates and does not incorporate the 2026 LiDAR campaign.

evidence.title: Almost 80% of the basin at 0–1% earthwork probability; dark earths widespread where earthworks are not
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states that "Almost 80% of the basin has a 0 to 1% of predicted probability" of earthwork presence per 1 km² cell, that these low-probability areas lie mostly in northwestern, northern, and central Amazonia, that higher-probability areas (≥25%) cover 1.41% of the basin and sit in the southwest, and that "Earth-building societies were very common in some parts of the basin, but they may not have occupied all of Amazonia." It adds that "Other types of domesticated landscapes, such as Amazonian Dark Earths, are widespread" in regions (e.g., central Amazonia) where the earthwork types it models are uncommon.
evidence.editorInference: Independent-in-method corroboration of AMZ-C020's 'limited, albeit impressive' earthwork extent and of the heterogeneous-Amazon attribution (AMZ-C016): the same research network that documents hotspots also models most of the basin as low-probability for this class of monument. Independence from SRC-WALKER-2023 is partial — different modelling teams, but overlapping site databases.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 7] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints)
limitations: Low predicted earthwork probability is not absence of occupation: the paper itself notes dark earths are widespread where earthworks are not.
Model trained on biased presence-only records; the 80% figure is a model output.

evidence.title: Nearly all ≥25%-probability cells fall in a 94,713 km² rectangle over Acre
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states that nearly all the highest-probability cells (≥25% predicted probability) occur in a 94,713 km² "rectangle that overlays a significant portion of the Brazilian state of Acre," and that southwestern Amazonia contains the earliest plant cultivation, the oldest anthropogenic soils, low-density urbanism, and now the highest concentration of earthworks. Table S2 gives 86% of the ≥25% area and 96% of the ≥50% area in southwestern Amazonia.
evidence.editorInference: This is the region the 2026 Aquiry survey (AMZ-C004) later flew; the two studies agree on where earthworks concentrate, while differing on how many (see AMZ-E025).
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 7] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints); table S2 [p. 62]
limitations: Model-derived concentration partly reflects where Acre deforestation has exposed earthworks; the observability covariates aim to correct this but cannot fully remove it.

evidence.title: 53 of 79 domesticated tree species significantly associated with modelled earthwork probability
evidence.sourceStatement: Using 1,676 forest plots and generalized linear models, the paper states that "53 of the 79 domesticated species showed significant association" with the predicted probability of earthwork presence — 35 increasing (e.g., Bertholletia excelsa, Theobroma cacao, Attalea phalerata) and 18 decreasing (e.g., Erisma japura, Oenocarpus bataua) — and in the abstract that it "identified 53 domesticated tree species significantly associated with earthwork occurrence probability, likely suggesting past management practices."
evidence.editorInference: Corroborates AMZ-C008's tree-domestication leg with a different response variable (modelled earthwork probability rather than distance to known sites), but the species list is Levis et al. 2017's own and the authors overlap, so this is not independent of SRC-LEVIS-2017; the McMichael 2017 post-Columbian-management objection (AMZ-E013) applies equally here.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 9] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints); abstract [p. 3]
limitations: Association with a modelled probability surface, not with dated archaeological sites.
Same species list and overlapping authorship as SRC-LEVIS-2017; not an independent group.
Cannot separate pre- from post-Columbian management (see AMZ-E013).

evidence.title: Known earthworks have mostly been found in deforested, road-accessible areas
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states: "Until now, pre-Columbian earthworks have mostly been discovered in deforested areas." and that observability covariates show "previously reported earthworks are mostly found near roads, which facilitate field research"; the supplement adds that only 9% of the 937 known earthworks lie inside indigenous lands and protected areas and that the highest known density is in the 'Arc of Deforestation'.
evidence.editorInference: A source-stated sampling bias, of the same kind AMZ-C021 records for palaeoecological cores — here on the positive side of the ledger.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 38] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints); also [p. 8], [p. 10]
limitations: Descriptive statement about the record's history, quantified only via the road-distance and tree-cover histograms (fig. S18).

evidence.title: Sampling bias in the recorded-site base that river-distance and site-type models are built on
evidence.sourceStatement: The paper states that "Until now, pre-Columbian earthworks have mostly been discovered in deforested areas," that recorded earthworks are mostly near roads, and that sampling of all Amazonian archaeological sites 'follows a similar pattern: a greater number of records in areas with greater accessibility and more intensive research histories'.
evidence.editorInference: Editor's inference: models over recorded sites (AMZ-C013 from 7,363 sites; AMZ-C020 from Walker's ML) inherit this accessibility bias unless corrected; Peripato's own correction is an observability sub-model. This narrows, without denying, what a river-distance gradient in recorded sites can establish about the unrecorded matrix.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 38], [p. 40] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints)
limitations: The source does not analyse SRC-MCMICHAEL-2025 or SRC-WALKER-2023; the transfer of its bias statement to those records is the editor's.

evidence.title: Independent restatement: Acre earthworks built AD 120–400; Mato Grosso earthworks AD 1250–1500
evidence.sourceStatement: The supplement states that radiocarbon dating of earthworks located in Acre "indicates their construction between 120 and 400 A.D." and that, by contrast, Mato Grosso earthworks are more recent, dating from 1250 to 1500 AD.
evidence.editorInference: Seconds AMZ-E003: the southwestern monument florescence is a millennium before Orellana and cannot be spent as contact-era corroboration of Carvajal; the later southern-rim dates (AMZ-C006) are the ones that overlap him. Secondary restatement citing others' dates, hence weak.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 38] via open-access accepted manuscript (White Rose eprints)
limitations: A literature summary (citing refs 14, 15), not new dating.

research.title: Blind, probability-stratified LiDAR test of the competing earthwork-density predictions
research.summary: Select LiDAR survey blocks at random within strata defined by the 2023 basin-wide probability surface (0–1%, 1–10%, 10–25%, ≥25%) and, inside the Aquiry area, by the 2026 study's regional model — choosing blocks before any archaeological knowledge of them is consulted and registering the selection. Fly and inspect each block with a fixed detection protocol and independent expert confirmation, then record earthworks per km² per stratum. Compare the observed densities with the densities each model implies for those strata. Observed densities in the 0–1% stratum at or near zero and rising monotonically with predicted probability would support AMZ-C028–C030 as calibrated; systematic under-prediction inside the Aquiry area would favour the 2026 regional total in AMZ-C004 over the basin-wide one, and the reverse would favour the lower. Either result narrows the several-fold spread between published earthwork totals that AMZ-E025 records.
research.informationGain: Directly calibrates two predictive models whose totals differ several-fold, using sampling chosen blind to promise — the earthwork counterpart of AMZ-R003, and the only way to tell whether the 24–30k regional figure and the 10–24k basin figure can both be right.
